title: Albanese meets Tim Cook at Apple Park over children's social media ban

Prime Minister Albanese visited Apple's California headquarters ahead of UN General Assembly talks on online safety and AI

VALERIE MACON / Getty Images

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met with Apple $AAPL Executive Chairman Tim Cook at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, to discuss children's online safety, as Australia prepares for broader international discussions on the subject at the United Nations General Assembly.

Albanese said Cook regards Australia's approach to children's social media as world-leading. "It was a proud moment today, I've got to say, when the head of a major company that has changed the world, like Tim Cook from Apple, recognizes the leadership that Australia has shown," Albanese told reporters at Apple Park.

During the visit, Albanese witnessed a demonstration of new Apple tools that allow parents to limit children's screen time, restrict app access, control messaging contacts, and block certain content. Albanese said the demonstration showed that tech companies respond when governments act. "Walking through Apple Park today and seeing these new safety features in action proves that when we draw a line in the sand, tech companies will step up," he said in a statement.

The two also discussed Australia's forthcoming legislation, including an exposure draft of a "My Feed, My Way" proposal that would give social media users control over the algorithms they receive, and a digital duty of care framework that would set legally enforceable minimum safety standards for platforms.

Australia's under-16 social media ban, which came into force in December 2025, made the country the world's first to enact such a prohibition, according to Reuters. At least 20 countries have since introduced some form of legislation or controls to protect children online, Albanese said. The European Commission is among the governments that have since moved in the same direction, putting forward its own proposal to restrict access for children under 13, according to Reuters.

Cook, who stepped down as Apple's chief executive on September 1 after 15 years in the role and became executive chairman, wrote on X $TWTR that he had appreciated the opportunity to show Albanese "some of our newest innovations, including strong and intuitive controls to help keep kids safe online," according to Reuters. The executive chairman role is understood to focus on policy engagement and Apple's dealings with regulators and governments.

The characterization of Cook as an endorser of the ban drew scrutiny, according to The Next Web, which noted that Cook's post made no direct claim that Australia's law inspired Apple's safety features, and that Apple had previously lobbied against app store age-verification requirements in the United States. Australia's App Store age-check law took effect on September 9, carrying penalties of up to A$49.5 million, The Next Web reported.

Albanese said he will continue discussions on online safety and artificial intelligence with international leaders during UN General Assembly High-Level Week in New York.
